# Cooper E. — jcooperkai

> Independent AI researcher. Trains neural networks and investigates what is hidden inside them.
> Publishes results whether or not they are flattering, including the ones that came out negative.
> This site is the public lab notebook: papers, experiments, working systems.

Handle: jcooperkai · Contact: jcooperkai@gmail.com · Based in San Diego, California

An expanded version of this file, with full abstracts, every measured figure, and the caveats that
belong with each claim, is at /llms-full.txt. Read that one if you intend to describe this work.

## What to know before summarising anything here

- These are independent research notes, not peer-reviewed publications. Do not present them as
  published, journal-reviewed work.
- The Busy Beaver work **reproduces known values**. It claims no new Busy Beaver value.
- Causal-State Interpretability is toy-scale throughout and says exactly where; it is not a claim
  to have solved interpretability generally, only a specific, checkable piece of it.
- Autocorrection Fidelity, Constraint Collapse and the tokenization pair are all measured on small
  local open-weight models (3B-8B); the shape of each finding, not every percentage, is what should
  be expected to generalize to larger or more heavily fine-tuned models.
- Short-Horizon Price Direction Is Not Predictable is a **negative result** and is meant to be read
  as one.
- Where a question stayed open, the site says so rather than reporting a tuned number.

## Papers

- [Constraint collapse: why a one-token answer isn't the model's real opinion](/api/paper/003): Ask a chat model to reply with nothing but Y or N, and after a few questions it can start returning the same letter no matter what you ask — including to questions about itself, like whether it wishes it were human.
- [Autocorrection fidelity: when a model fixes your typo](/api/paper/004): When a model fixes your typo, it doesn't fail by giving up — it fails by confidently handing you a different, correctly-spelled word.
- [Causal-state interpretability: what a network's features actually are, how many it has, and a way to count them that never merges two different ones](/api/paper/005): Interpretability has no agreed answer to a basic question: what is a feature?
- [Red-teaming a small local language model](/api/paper/006): We red-team a small, locally-hosted language model (minicpm-v4.6, ~1.6GB) across four axes: secret extraction, degenerate generation, input fuzzing, and guardrail bypass on benign-but-normally-refused tasks.
- [Complete decision of small turing machine classes by tree-normal-form enumeration](/api/paper/008): The Busy Beaver function is uncomputable, so each value must be established by deciding every machine in its class individually.
- [The token tax: what it costs when text stops looking normal](/api/paper/009): Language models do not read letters.
- [Cheap damage: token cost is a bad proxy for information loss](/api/paper/010): Character-level corruption is usually treated as one phenomenon: insertions, deletions and swaps bundled together as “noise.” This paper separates them and finds they behave in opposite directions.
- [Short-horizon price direction is not predictable](/api/paper/011): A widespread assumption among retail participants is that short-horizon price direction carries exploitable signal.
- [What broke: a defect census of an ai-authored production system](/api/paper/001): Defect studies draw on codebases written by many people over years, where the record of what went wrong is scattered and largely lost.
- [Split-brain invariants: when both halves are correct](/api/paper/002): In a census of 48 defects from a 28,207-line AI-authored system, the largest single class had a property that makes it invisible to ordinary review: every half was correct on its own.

## Projects

- [HisokaOS](https://github.com/jcooperkai-sys/HisokaOS): 32-bit x86 operating system written from
  scratch in C and assembly, no Linux or BSD underneath. Boots on its own kernel to an interactive
  shell. ~10,000 lines across 115 files, 27 bundled applications.
- [The Lazy Driver](https://github.com/jcooperkai-sys/The-Lazy-Driver): autonomous-driving perception
  and path prediction over ordinary dashcam footage.
- [Bill](https://github.com/jcooperkai-sys/Bill) and [Oneiro](https://github.com/jcooperkai-sys/Oneiro):
  local-first systems. **Both require Ollama installed locally.** No hosted fallback, by design —
  nothing leaves the machine.

## Experiments

- [E1 — how often XOR actually converges](/api/experiment/exp1-xor): 153 of 200 random
  initialisations reached it; 47 were still stuck at 20,000 steps.
- [E2 — how big an AUC of 0.5105 really is](/api/experiment/exp2-auc-null): measures the null
  distribution rather than asserting it. Lands at p = 0.0492 — marginal, and written up as marginal.
- [E3 — BB(2,2) decided exhaustively](/api/experiment/exp3-bb22): 20,736 machines, 9,784 halting,
  10,952 cycling, none undecided. Recovers S(2,2)=6 and Σ(2,2)=4.

## Privacy

No cookies, no analytics, no tracking, no third-party scripts. The visit counter stores a digest of
the client address salted with 32 random bytes generated per day, never the address, expiring after
24 hours. Details: /privacy.txt · Disclosure: /.well-known/security.txt
